I opened a vanguard account a few months ago and put $3k in the VTI fund, owing that I subscribe to the theory that picking individual stocks is no better than betting on horse races.

Now I find myself in a position where I'm making good money at my job, and I want to buy a house. I've priced out my total PITI payments and budgeted for a house that I can afford while paying all my other expenses and still saving about 4% of my total income every year.

The question that arises is this: Why would it ever be advisable to put money into an investment account while you have a loan such as a mortgage? I calculated the interest saved if I make extra payments on the mortgage. A dozen payments of just $500 a month (say I rented a room to a friend for a year) saves me over $15,000 in interest if I can manage it in the first couple years of the loan.

It seems to me that chucking money at uncertain investments is foolish when you could pay down real, set in stone loans like mortgages early on and know you will save thousands of dollars.

For reference I am using a spreadsheet that calculates mortgage amortization with paydown. I'm looking at putting money in the "extra payments" column instead of "investing" it.

Some advice from an old guy who is a bit evangelistic on the subject - make saving/investing a regular habit AND retire all debts as quickly as possible. Both are necessary and deserve equal focus. You must make saving a habit - it needs to be practiced regularly no matter what your income and no matter what your debts because there is a tendency to make lame excuses for not doing it (just ask your friends why they are not saving). Even a few dollars with each paycheck helps. Complementing this, interest is a burden that steals from you every day. It is worth any sacrifice to retire all debts as quickly as possible-again even if you have can only scratch a couple dollars extra per month. If you are making good money this should not be hard but does require consistent discipline. Live with a little modestly (At this point in life I could have the Porsche that I always wanted but life has convinced me that my Subaru is more that adequate to get me to work - Yes, I still like going to work.) Make paying off your house a priority. The beauty of this is that you can use the equity to consolidate all of your other debts at a low and possibly deductible interest rate - I maintain a Home Equity Line of Credit at 5.5%. I go with the automatic payment option because it protects your credit and gives a slightly better rate BUT like all debts I make bulk payments against the principle as quickly as I am able.

Picking individual stocks is a game that is stacked against the average Joe (like me). I have had my money in a number of Vanguard funds (most of which are rather aggressive) for about 20 years. It took a little time to learn the language and which ones were best but the annual rate of return that I have received for the last 18 years has fluctuated between 11 and 13%! (that includes those months during the recession) Yeah, there are local fluctuations over time - for ex. over the last two months I lost ~$ 120,000 - but I have already regained $110,000 of that back. When it goes down YOU ABSOLUTELY MUST RESIST ANY TEMPTATION TO PULL YOUR MONEY OUT!

A little math leads to an interesting speculation - home equity line of credit costing 5.5% per annum vs - investment for an 11-13% return per annum. Also, and this is important, never take the advice of a stranger esp an old one and never rely on anyone who does not have a stake in the outcome. Good luck!
